chapters.title: Chapter 4: AIS and TIS, the Full Picture of Your Financial Year

lessons.title: What AIS Captures: Interest, Dividends, Shares, Mutual Funds and High-Value Transactions

children.text: Most people open AIS looking for their salary and TDS, find them, and close it. That misses the point. AIS earns its keep in the entries you did not expect: the savings account interest you never thought about, the ₹900 dividend from shares you forgot you held, the mutual fund you redeemed to pay for a wedding, the credit card bills you paid. This lesson walks through what AIS captures, where each piece comes from, and what it does and does not mean for your tax.

body.text: AIS captures two kinds of information: income you must report, and large transactions that show how you spend and invest. The first changes your tax. The second only has to make sense next to your income.

children.text: Interest: SFT-016

Banks, cooperative banks, post offices and NBFCs report interest paid or credited to you during the year under SFT-016. This includes savings account interest, fixed and recurring deposit interest and post office scheme interest. Crucially, it is reported whether or not any TDS was deducted.

That is why interest is the most common gap between Form 26AS and AIS. Priya's SBI FD paid ₹38,000 with no TDS, so Form 26AS shows nothing, but AIS shows the full ₹38,000 under SFT-016. Her ICICI Bank FD appears twice, once under TDS-194A and once under SFT-016, and TIS removes the duplicate.
Dividends: SFT-015

Companies report every dividend they distribute under SFT-015, regardless of amount. If a dividend from one company crosses ₹10,000 in the year, TDS is deducted too, and the same dividend also appears under TDS-194. A dividend of ₹900 from a PSU stock you bought years ago will still show up.
Shares and Other Securities: SFT-017

Stock exchanges, depositories, clearing corporations and registrars report purchases and sales of securities under SFT-017, with sub-codes for listed equity shares and other instruments. For sales, AIS can show the quantity, the sales consideration, a cost of acquisition and the holding period, which is used to classify the asset as short term or long term.

body.text: Do not treat the SFT-017 figures as your capital gains. For transfers out of your demat account that are not normal exchange sales, the reported sale consideration can be an estimate based on the best available price, such as the end-of-day price. The cost of acquisition may be missing or incomplete. Always compute gains from your broker's tax P&L, such as Zerodha Console or Groww's capital gains report, and use AIS only to check that every sale is accounted for.

children.text: Mutual Fund Units: SFT-018

Purchases and redemptions of mutual fund units are reported under SFT-018 by registrars such as CAMS and KFintech, and by depositories for units held in demat. The same redemption can be reported by both the registrar and the depository, and the system deduplicates them. Priya's ₹2,40,000 redemption appears under SFT-018. Like shares, the figure is sale value, not gain.

children.text: High-Value Transactions: SFT-001 to SFT-013
The earlier SFT codes report large transactions. None of them is income. They exist so the department can compare how much money moves through your hands with how much income you declare.

body.caption: High-value transactions a salaried person is most likely to trigger (reporting thresholds per financial year unless stated)

cells: Cash deposits or withdrawals in current accounts
Cash deposits in accounts other than current accounts, such as savings
₹1 lakh or more in cash, or ₹10 lakh or more by any other mode
Purchase of bonds or debentures from the issuer
Purchase of shares from the issuing company, such as in an IPO
Purchase of foreign currency, including forex cards and travellers cheques
Purchase or sale of immovable property
Cash payment for goods or services to a business that is audited

body.text: Thresholds are aggregates, not per account. Depositing ₹6 lakh of cash in one bank and ₹5 lakh in another adds up to ₹11 lakh, and each reporting bank's data is combined against your PAN.

children.text: Other Information
The last section of AIS collects data from sources outside the TDS and SFT systems. The entries you are most likely to see:
Salary details
from Annexure II of your employer's last-quarter salary TDS statement, which shows the breakup your employer reported.
Outward foreign remittances
reported in Form 15CC, such as money sent abroad for a child's education or an overseas investment.
Interest on income tax refund
, which is taxable income in the year you receive it.
GST turnover
, if you are registered under GST as a freelancer or business owner.
Two Checks to Run on Every AIS

columns.label: Completeness: is all my income in my return?
points: Every SFT-016 interest entry, including savings accounts
Every SFT-017 and SFT-018 sale, turned into a gain or loss
Interest on refund and any rent with TDS
Missed income here is the most common reason for a mismatch notice

columns.label: Consistency: does my spending fit my income?
points: Big mutual fund or share purchases
Nothing to report here, but keep records of where the money came from

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Name the code
body.question: Vikas, a salesman in Kanpur, deposits cash from a family wedding into his savings accounts during FY 2025-26. Under which SFT code would this be reported if it crosses the threshold?
body.explanation: SFT-004 covers cash deposits in accounts other than current accounts, such as savings accounts, at ₹10 lakh or more in aggregate. SFT-003 is for current accounts and SFT-005 for time deposits.

body.title: Add up the aggregate
body.prompt: Vikas deposits ₹6,50,000 in cash into his SBI savings account and ₹4,00,000 into his Canara Bank savings account during FY 2025-26. What is his aggregate cash deposit for SFT-004 purposes?
body.explanation: ₹6,50,000 + ₹4,00,000 = ₹10,50,000. That crosses the ₹10 lakh aggregate threshold, so it will appear in his AIS even though neither bank alone received ₹10 lakh. It is not income by itself, but he should be able to explain the source of the cash.

body.title: Sale value is not gain
body.prompt: Sunita's AIS shows an SFT-017 sale of listed equity shares with sales consideration of ₹3,20,000. Her Zerodha tax P&L shows she bought those shares for ₹2,60,000. What capital gain does she need to report, before any exemption?
body.explanation: Capital gain = sale value minus cost = ₹3,20,000 minus ₹2,60,000 = ₹60,000. Whether it is short term or long term depends on how long she held the shares. The ₹3,20,000 in AIS is not her income.

body.title: Property threshold
body.textWithBlank: A property registrar reports a purchase or sale of immovable property under SFT-012 when the transaction value is ₹___ lakh or more.
body.explanation: SFT-012 applies to each purchase or sale of immovable property of ₹30 lakh or more, reported by the Registrar or Sub-Registrar.

body.title: Radhika's credit card entry
body.scenario: Radhika, a sales manager in Pune earning ₹14 lakh a year, sees an SFT-006 entry in her AIS: credit card payments of ₹11,20,000 during FY 2025-26, all paid by net banking. Most of it was work travel that her employer reimbursed. She worries this will be treated as extra income or trigger a notice.
body.prompt: Does this entry change her tax? What, if anything, should she do?
body.modelAnswer: No. A credit card payment is spending, not income, so SFT-006 does not add to her taxable income. The entry is correct, so she does not need to give feedback disputing it. What matters is whether her spending is consistent with her resources. Since ₹11.2 lakh is large relative to a ₹14 lakh salary, she should keep her employer's reimbursement records, card statements and expense claims, so she can explain the pattern if she is ever asked. Reimbursements for genuine business expenses are not income, but personal spending funded by undeclared income would be a problem.

cards.definition: Cash deposits in savings and other non-current accounts, ₹10 lakh or more in aggregate in a year.
Time deposits other than renewals, ₹10 lakh or more in aggregate in a year.
Credit card bill payments: ₹1 lakh or more in cash, or ₹10 lakh or more by any other mode.
Purchase or sale of immovable property of ₹30 lakh or more, reported by the registrar.
Dividends paid by companies, every amount.
Interest paid or credited by banks, post offices and NBFCs, with or without TDS.
Purchase and sale of securities such as listed shares and bonds.
Purchase and sale of mutual fund units, reported by registrars and depositories.

points: SFT-016 reports all interest and SFT-015 all dividends, even when no TDS was deducted.
SFT-017 and SFT-018 report sales of shares and mutual funds. The sale value is not your gain, and reported cost can be missing or estimated.
SFT-001 to SFT-013 report large transactions such as cash deposits, property deals and credit card payments. They are not income.
High-value thresholds are aggregates across all your accounts, not per account.
Other information includes salary breakup, foreign remittances and interest on refunds.
Use AIS for two checks: is all my income reported, and does my spending fit my declared income?

body.text: This lesson is for education only and reflects SFT codes and thresholds as of September 2026. Thresholds may be revised under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 for later years. Names and amounts are illustrative. For your specific situation, consult a chartered accountant.
